title: Anthropic gives METR researchers employee-like access to audit its models from the inside
summary: Anthropic announced on Thursday, October 15, that it has onboarded six employees from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models, with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools “roughly on par” with what its own risk-assessment teams see. Outside narrow categories such as customer data, attorney-client privilege, and model-architecture details, staff are encouraged to share information with them as with a fellow alignment colleague. METR will publish its own analysis of Anthropic’s risk levels, incidents, and practices; Anthropic cannot veto publication but may require redactions in those predefined categories, and METR may say publicly whether it believes the redactions were justified. The arrangement sits at the top of a three-tier evaluator system; SecureBio and Accenture (with Faculty) are at earlier, more limited tiers, and Anthropic says it is in early talks with Hugging Face and others. The company says it is not funding METR’s work, and that the step follows its White House Accord pledge and CEO Dario Amodei’s call to embed independent evaluators.

title: Simons Foundation, OpenAI, and Anthropic put $15 million behind helping mathematicians navigate AI proofs
summary: The Simons Foundation announced on October 15 a partnership with Anthropic and OpenAI committing $15 million in combined funding and resources so mathematicians can evaluate AI-assisted results, learn new tools, share perspectives, and shape collective standards for AI use. The foundation will manage and award the money through an open call for proposals supporting workshops and related programs. OpenAI separately said it is contributing $5 million to the initiative and will provide model and compute access to supported researchers; Anthropic and OpenAI will also supply tools and compute that can extend beyond mathematics into basic science. Foundation president David Spergel said the community—not any single company—should drive how the tools are evaluated and adopted. The Independent and other outlets noted the gift follows backlash after OpenAI published a large batch of experimental AI-generated proofs that mathematicians said overwhelmed traditional review.

title: NYC Comptroller Mark Levine urges Anthropic to pause its IPO until AI safety and governance catch up
summary: New York City Comptroller Mark Levine wrote Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on October 14 urging the company to pause its planned IPO until it fully and transparently addresses AI safety, governance, and development-pace concerns, a letter his office published with October 15 coverage. Levine oversees public pension funds with more than $325 billion in assets. He cites Amodei’s September essay calling to slow capability gains, draft S-1 risk language that reportedly warns of catastrophic or existential risks, and governance arrangements that may concentrate control with founders and trustees. Before going public, he asks Anthropic to disclose specific audits and controls, their scope, a timeline, and how those steps would support slowing capability development. Bloomberg Law and Reuters reported the call; Levine requested a written response.

title: Dow jumps about 556 points as investors rotate out of tech; S&P 500 rises 0.3% and Nasdaq claws back 0.1%
summary: U.S. indexes closed higher Thursday, October 15, after a shaky session that still left AI and chip names under pressure, AP News and market wrap reports say. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose about 556 points, or 1.1%, led by consumer-related names; the S&P 500 gained 0.3% and pulled closer to its recent record; and the Nasdaq Composite finished up about 0.1% after erasing steeper early losses. Investors rotated toward Treasuries and away from tech: the 10-year yield fell sharply, and the S&P tech sector still finished lower even as the broader market rose. The bounce followed Wednesday’s hot CPI print that had sent the Nasdaq and S&P to their worst days since July. Nvidia fell nearly 2% on the day after a roughly 3% pullback Wednesday, while Apple slipped about 0.3%.

title: CoreWeave rebounds about 6% after Nvidia’s Jensen Huang says its finances look stronger, not bailout-bound
summary: After Wednesday’s roughly 15% plunge on debt worries, CoreWeave reversed course Thursday and closed up about 5.9% to 6%, market wrap accounts say, as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang pushed back on bailout chatter. Speaking around a Stockholm appearance, Huang said he did not believe CoreWeave would need a bailout from Nvidia and that its cost of capital was improving—an important vote for a heavily leveraged AI infrastructure name that has become a test case for circular financing concerns. Hyperscalers steadied as well, with Microsoft up about 1.1% and Oracle about 3%, while the broader chip selloff slowed: Broadcom was down about 0.6% and AMD about 1.5%, with Micron up roughly 1.9%. Nvidia itself still finished lower, about 1.8%. The swing underscores how tightly AI infrastructure stocks now trade on both credit fears and supplier reassurances.

title: Nvidia slides into correction territory, down about 12% from its peak as AI spending jitters linger
summary: Nvidia, still among the world’s most valuable public companies, closed near the mid-$210s on Thursday after an eight-session slide that market commentary pegged at roughly 11–12% from a recent peak near $243—enough to put the stock in common correction territory. Hotter inflation and worries about borrowing costs for the AI buildout have weighed on chips and AI infrastructure all week; Nvidia alone was described in trader chatter as having shed on the order of $700 billion-plus in market value across the stretch. Support levels around $210–$213 drew heavy attention. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF finished down about 0.3% Thursday even as the Dow rallied, highlighting how the AI trade can lag a broader rebound.

title: NVIDIA opens Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B multimodal agent model, plus Bolt edge variants
summary: NVIDIA on October 15 released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter multimodal mixture-of-experts model aimed at always-on enterprise agents that need instruction following, tool use, multistep workflows, and visual understanding of pages, PDFs, charts, and tables. The company positions it as about one-fifth the size of its largest reasoning model while matching that class on specialized agentic tasks, and as up to 5× faster than the next-best open peer in its Artificial Analysis class comparison. Organizations can post-train it on their own data; early customizers named in NVIDIA’s post include Scale AI, AfterQuery, Mercor, CrowdStrike, Salesforce, Perplexity, and others. Two edge companions arrive as Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: a 74B-A9B 24GB variant available now for local RTX/DGX Spark agent work, and a 4GB E4B conversational edge model due October 23. Super VL weights are on Hugging Face, OpenRouter, ModelScope, and as NVIDIA NIM.

title: OpenAI’s Rosalind Academic Plan gives U.S. university labs free seats and GPT-Rosalind access
summary: OpenAI on October 15 introduced the Rosalind Academic Plan for eligible U.S. university labs, offering up to 30 ChatGPT Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months plus access to GPT-Rosalind—its life-sciences model and Rosalind workbench for chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and related scientific tool use—subject to trusted-access approval. Research data shared under the plan is not used to train OpenAI models by default; API access and credits are not included. PIs and lab leads without an existing Enterprise agreement apply through trusted access; labs at universities with Enterprise must go through their institutional process. OpenAI cites early academic users including labs at UCSF, Stanford/Arc Institute, and others, and says it verifies institutional legitimacy, PI identity, research intent, and a designated safety contact before activation.

title: LLMs that evolve specialist heuristics beat prior AI methods on 36 combinatorial optimization benchmarks
summary: Researchers from Nanyang Technological University and collaborators report in Nature Machine Intelligence (published October 1, 2026) a framework called LACE—LLM-driven Algorithm Construction via Complementary Evolution—that splits algorithm design into a verified input/output/tool/heuristic interface and then evolves a portfolio of specialist heuristics under time budgets. Across 36 classical CO-Bench problems, LACE averaged 0.945 versus 0.870 for the strongest prior LLM-based method and 0.571 for direct prompting with no framework. On four structurally new problems, LACE scored 0.97–0.99 while five existing LLM baselines failed to produce any feasible algorithm. Code and data are open on GitHub and Zenodo. The work targets manufacturing, logistics, healthcare operations, and energy scheduling where hand-designed heuristics usually take months of expert iteration.

title: Google’s open MedGemma medical vision-language models land in Nature Medicine
summary: A Google Research and DeepMind team reports in Nature Medicine (published October 6, 2026) MedGemma, a family of medical vision-language foundation models built on Gemma 3—including multimodal 4B and 27B variants plus a 27B text model—and MedSigLIP, a medically tuned vision encoder. On out-of-distribution tasks the authors report gains of 2.6–10% in medical image question answering, 15.5–18.1% in chest X-ray finding classification, and 10.8% in agentic evaluations versus the base models, while keeping general Gemma capabilities largely intact. Fine-tuning MedGemma was more data-efficient than fine-tuning base Gemma 3 on several medical tasks. Models and example code are released via Google’s Health AI Developer Foundations; the authors stress clinical validation remains essential before real-world use.

title: Moroccan teens say AI helps them learn—and warn about the ‘laziness paradox’
summary: A mixed-methods study in Discover Education (published October 6, 2026) surveyed 150 secondary students in Morocco’s Casablanca-Settat region and interviewed 12 of them about AI-assisted learning. Students reported positive perceptions across learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, with a strong link between perceived outcomes and motivation. ChatGPT was the most-used tool, usually on personal phones as a homework aid. Qualitative themes included clearer explanations and less stress, conditional trust via cross-checking course materials, worry about AI mistakes in STEM, and a “laziness paradox” when ready-made answers reduce cognitive effort. The authors urge schools to teach responsible use—critique and verify, don’t ban blindly—and to redesign homework so students evaluate AI output instead of submitting it raw.

title: Read beside yesterday’s UMD trial: AI can light the spark, but you still have to do the reps
summary: Yesterday’s sheet carried a University of Maryland–led randomized trial of 2,379 undergraduates in which course-integrated generative AI tutor access was associated with lower final grades and less LMS participation. Set that next to today’s Moroccan classroom study: teens feel more motivated and organized with AI, yet name the laziness trap themselves. The GROKI takeaway for Friday stays practical. Use the model to clarify a stuck step, then close the chat and finish the problem in your own handwriting. Check answers against the textbook or a teacher before you trust a fluent reply. Motivation that outsources the struggle tends to fade; motivation that uses AI as a coach tends to stick.

title: Tonight at the Cajundome: Kevin Gates headlines HOT 107.9’s Birthday Bash 23, 8 p.m.
summary: Live Nation and HOT 107.9 present Birthday Bash 23 featuring Kevin Gates with special guests Bun B, Rob49, Slim Thug, Mouse & Level, and Wochee, hosted by DJ Sexy Lex, tonight—Friday, October 16—at 8 p.m. at the Cajundome. Lafayette Travel’s October events guide and Live Nation list the show; Cajundome.com carries venue policies. It is also the start of UL Lafayette’s Family Weekend (October 16–18), with the Ragin’ Cajuns hosting Troy on Saturday, October 17.

title: Saturday at River Ranch Town Square: The Big Easel outdoor fine art show, from 9 a.m.
summary: The Big Easel returns Saturday, October 17, in River Ranch Town Square, Lafayette Travel notes. Established in 2009 and now in its 17th year, the outdoor fine art event gives local and regional artists a platform; listings put hours around 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. with music, dance, and food alongside the art. Organizers describe it as bringing artists and the community together through creativity and conversation under the oaks.

title: Saturday at the Heymann Center: Mistletoe Market of Lafayette, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
summary: Start Christmas shopping Saturday, October 17, at the Mistletoe Market of Lafayette at the Heymann Performing Arts / Convention Center, 1373 S. College Road. Festival listings put general admission at 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., with roughly 80–90 vendors from Louisiana and Texas, giveaways, and holiday goods; some listings note earlier VIP hours. Check current admission details before you go. Lafayette Travel’s Friday guide also flags Vermilionville’s La Table Française this morning at 8:30 a.m.

title: Saturday night at Rock’n’Bowl de Lafayette: Cypress Valley Band, 9 p.m.
summary: Cypress Valley Band brings zydeco and Cajun to Rock’n’Bowl de Lafayette, 905 Jefferson Street, on Saturday, October 17, at 9 p.m., the venue calendar and Advocate weekend music listings say. Tickets have been listed around $17. Pair it with Saturday’s daytime art and market stops, or with UL’s home football game against Troy the same afternoon.

title: Saturday at the Main Library: Makerspace Open Access, 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
summary: Lafayette Public Library’s Main Library Makerspace/Tech Lab holds Open Access on Saturday, October 17, from 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a noon–1:00 p.m. lunch closure, the library’s LibCal listing says. The session is open to all ages with no registration required—handy for Family Weekend visitors who want a free, hands-on afternoon between the Big Easel and evening music.
